feature.name: Smoking Hills
aka: Smoking Hills and lower Horton River
feature.description: The white streaks are bare badland slopes. Here the lower Horton River and the Franklin Bay sea cliffs cut up to 200 m into soft Cretaceous shale, and the unvegetated gullies stand out pale against green tundra. The shale holds lignite and pyrite-rich, sulphurous beds that catch fire by themselves when erosion exposes them. They were already smoking when Franklin's expedition named the hills in 1826, and the fumes have acidified nearby ponds. Around 1750 a Horton meander broke through the coastal bluffs into Franklin Bay, building a small delta and abandoning about 100 km of the old channel to Harrowby Bay.

feature.name: Kgalagadi Fence Line
feature.description: A dead-straight north-south line on the 20th meridian across the red Kalahari dunes, about 110 km long, between Union's End and Mata-Mata on the Auob River. East of it is South Africa's Kalahari Gemsbok National Park, part of the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park, which looks paler and smoother. West of it are Namibian sheep and cattle farms, which look darker and blotchier: most likely because livestock crop the grass, leaving more bare red sand and letting dark shrubs spread. feature.name: Richardson Mountains
feature.description: A narrow north-south spine of bare, rumpled grey-brown tundra ridges, over 300 km long, straddling the Yukon-Northwest Territories border west of the Mackenzie Delta. To the east it drops sharply to the flat, lake-speckled Peel Plateau, and to the west it gives way to the rolling Porcupine country. entries.response: Tinigua's deal: it's a national park (no clearing allowed anywhere), but since the FARC left after the 2016 peace deal, land grabbers, cattle ranchers and coca growers backed by dissident armed groups have cleared much of it (about 40% of its 1990s forest gone; Mongabay, es.wikipedia). There is no official no-deforestation subset that matches what you see: the La Macarena management area (AMEM) only zones its districts (preservation / recovery / production); the three parks are already the strictest category in full. So I traced the visible intact forest instead (forest mask on recent Google imagery, kept only where >= 85% of a 2.5 km window is unbroken forest) and clipped it to the parks: new feature 'Sierra de la Macarena Forests' (~7,400 km2, vis_zoom 7.5) = the serranía and its eastern lowland forest, the intact northern ~quarter of Tinigua, and Picachos minus its cleared SE corner. The description explains the Tinigua clearing.

feature.name: Sierra de la Macarena Forests
aka: Sierra de la Macarena National Park
Cordillera de los Picachos National Park
feature.description: The still-intact rainforest of three adjoining Colombian national parks, about 230 km across: the Serranía de la Macarena, an isolated tabletop range rising out of the Llanos with lowland forest stretching east to the Guayabero, the northern part of Tinigua between it and the Andes, and the forested Andean foothills of Cordillera de los Picachos. All three are national parks, the strictest zone of the Macarena special management area (AMEM), where no clearing is allowed at all, so the legal boundaries are not where the forest ends. Since the FARC demobilised after the 2016 peace deal, land grabbers, cattle ranchers and coca growers, often backed by dissident armed groups, have cleared large parts of Tinigua (it had lost about 40% of its 1990s forest by the 2020s) and the south-east of Picachos; those cut-over areas now look like the pasture mosaic outside, and this outline follows the edge of the forest that remains rather than the park lines.
feature.look_for: Dark unbroken forest block with a ragged edge against a speckled pasture mosaic
